home.intro:
Product engineer. I design and ship systems end to end, and what I build has no sector: a company's operations, an election, a cultural product, a learning platform. What interests me sits where a product decision and a technical decision turn out to be the same decision.

Over the past year: a multi-tenant SaaS platform in production for many clients, a civic platform, fourteen reference implementations for people learning to ship, and technical direction of a cultural product.

decisions.label: How I work
decisions.intro: Six steps, from the first framing through to running it. They adapt to your product, whatever its domain and its size.

one.title: I start from the problem and who has it
one.body: I identify who has the problem, what it costs them today, and the number that will say it is solved. I also note what stays out of scope. That written framing then acts as the arbiter: every request arriving mid-project is measured against it instead of reopening a debate.

two.title: I sort constraints into negotiable and non-negotiable
two.body: Usage volume and shape, expected availability, the nature of the data and the rules that apply to it, systems already in place, team, budget, deadline. The non-negotiable pile rules out most architectures before anyone debates them. For each remaining choice I note whether it is reversible: decide fast on what can be undone, slowly on what cannot.

three.title: I make at least two options stand up before choosing
three.body: Compared against the criteria set in the first step, not against the preferences of whoever speaks loudest. Then one written decision, with what it rules out and why. A team can move without me, and the debate does not come back three months later under a different name.

four.title: I decide form alongside the model
four.body: Hierarchy, typography, rhythm, density: these are product decisions, taken with the data model rather than after it. I start from the states, empty, loading, error, insufficient rights, because they are what reveal what the product actually has to be able to do.

five.title: I ship the riskiest slice first, end to end
five.body: Not the easiest. A thin but complete slice, all the way to production, puts the plan against reality while there is still time to change it. What follows is execution.

six.title: I measure, I operate, and I stay
six.body: Instrumentation from the first release, read against the objective set in the first step. Operations are designed rather than added: logs, alerts, recovery procedures. A system that only holds while I am watching it is not finished.
